title: What Is an Option?
subtitle: A right - not an obligation - to buy or sell an asset
openingQuestion: What is the core difference between an option and futures/forward?
openingOptions: An option is a RIGHT to transact; futures/forward are an obligation
An option is only used for stocks
An option is always cheaper than futures
There is no real difference, just different names for the same one thing
explanation: An option grants the buyer a right - but not an obligation - to buy (a call) or sell (a put) an asset at a set price (the strike price) on or before an expiration date. The option buyer pays a fee called the premium for this right; if it isn't favorable, they can simply choose not to exercise it.

realWorldExample.description: CBOE is the world's largest options exchange, where investors buy and sell options on thousands of stocks and indices every day.

quiz.question: Why is an option compared to a kind of financial 'insurance'?
options: The buyer pays a fixed fee for protection, with the maximum loss capped at that fee
Because insurance companies themselves are the issuers of options
Because an option always turns a profit, so it's safe like insurance
An option has nothing to do with insurance, it's purely a speculative tool
quiz.explanation: Like an insurance policy: you pay a premium (fee) for the right to be protected if an unfavorable event occurs. If that event doesn't happen, you only lose the premium.

quiz.question: An investor buys both a call option and a put option at the same strike price and same expiration on the same stock (a "straddle" strategy). What are they betting on?
options: Betting the stock price will remain completely unchanged until expiration
A sharp move in either direction - standing still means losing on both
Betting on a sharp rise, since a call is always worth more than a put
Betting on a sharp fall, since a put fully protects the portfolio
quiz.explanation: A straddle is a strategy betting on VOLATILITY rather than a specific direction of price movement - suited to when an investor expects a major upcoming event to create sharp price swings.

quiz.question: How is an option buyer similar to an insurance buyer?
options: Both pay a fee upfront for protection against a bad scenario
Both get the fee refunded in full if the risk doesn't ever materialize
Both are obligated to perform the contract at maturity
Both are only compensated after a loss has already occurred
quiz.explanation: A premium is like an insurance fee: forfeited if not needed, but in exchange it caps potential loss. The difference is that an option also allows profiting if price runs in the right direction, while insurance does not.

quiz.question: Buying a call and a put at the same time, same strike, same expiration, is what strategy?
options: Doubling the profit if price moves the right direction
Fully hedging away all price-movement risk
Betting price will stay flat around the chosen strike
Betting on a sharp move, regardless of direction
quiz.explanation: This is a straddle. A sharp move in either direction produces a leg profitable enough to cover both premiums. Its enemy is a flat, sideways market - which loses both fees.

quiz.question: What is the maximum risk to an option buyer?
options: Exactly the premium paid, no more
The value of the entire option contract
Unlimited if the price moves against the bet
The gap between the strike and the market price
quiz.explanation: This asymmetry is what makes options attractive: loss is capped, gain is not. But most options expire worthless, so that cap gets hit fairly often.

keyTakeaways: Option: a right (not an obligation) to buy/sell at the strike price
Premium: the fee paid for the right, and the buyer's maximum risk
An option behaves like a form of priceable financial insurance

practicePrompt.question: You buy a contract that lets you (but doesn't require you to) buy VNM stock at VND 80,000 within the next 3 months. If the market price falls to VND 70,000, you can simply choose not to exercise the contract and only lose the fee already paid. This 'can choose not to perform' feature is the core distinguishing characteristic of which derivative type?
options: This is a feature of a Forward, since both parties are obligated to perform the contract at maturity
An Option is a right, not an obligation, to trade at the strike price; the most you lose is the premium
This is a feature of Futures, since the contract is standardized and exchange-traded
Every derivative contract type has this feature, there's nothing special about an Option
practicePrompt.explanation: Option: a right (not an obligation) to buy/sell at the strike price. This is the core difference from a Forward and Futures (where both sides must perform) - an option buyer only loses at most the premium paid if they choose not to exercise.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Find the price of a real option
application.message: The lesson already gave a real example of how to read the VN30F1M price board - see the 'Real-world example' section above. Now open a real derivatives price board and identify the elements you've learned.
application.secondary: Looking at a real price board makes the option concept much less abstract.

sections.text: An option differs fundamentally from a forward and futures in one key way: it gives the buyer a RIGHT, not an OBLIGATION, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a set price (the strike price) on or before an expiration date. If unfavorable, the buyer simply doesn't exercise that right.

This right isn't free. The option buyer must pay a fee called the premium at the moment of purchase - regardless of whether they later exercise the right. This is exactly what makes an option comparable to financial insurance: you pay a fixed fee for the right to be protected against an unfavorable price move, and your maximum risk is limited to that premium paid - you never lose more.

An interesting strategy is a straddle: buying both a call option and a put option at the same strike price, same expiration date, on the same stock. The investor isn't betting price will rise or fall, but that it will move SHARPLY in either direction - often used ahead of a major event such as an earnings report. If price stays near the strike, both options lose value and the investor loses both premiums paid.

items: Call option: the right to BUY at the strike price
Put option: the right to SELL at the strike price
Premium: the upfront fee for the right, and also the buyer's maximum risk
CBOE (Chicago Board Options Exchange): the world's largest options exchange

sections.text: Real-world example: reading the VN30F1M derivatives price board

items: Although Vietnam doesn't yet have a public stock options market like the US, the VN30F1M futures contract uses the same price-board-reading logic: contract price, required margin, open interest

For actual options (common in the US market), the two numbers to identify on the price board are the strike price (the price to exercise the right) and the premium (the price to buy the option) - the premium is the amount paid upfront, the strike is the price you're entitled to buy/sell at in the future
The initial margin for the VN30F1M futures contract is about 20% of contract value, giving a maximum leverage of about 1:5

sections.label: How to look it up yourself
sections.text: Open the "Derivatives" section of a Vietnamese securities company's app to see the VN30F1M; to see a real stock's option chain, look it up on international sites like Yahoo Finance with a US stock ticker (e.g. AAPL).

lines: An option gives you favorable asymmetry: capped risk, uncapped potential gain - but the price of that asymmetry is exactly the premium.
